examples.analytical: The psalmist joyfully sings praise, moving from lament to thanksgiving in the closing verses.

nuance.analogy: Joyfully is like a child running to the door when a friend arrives: the whole body shows the gladness.
nuance.etymology: From joyful plus the adverb suffix -ly, from joy and the Old French joie.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'joy-FUL-ly.'
Saying 'joyly' by dropping the f.
Using it where 'happily' is more natural in a casual context.

senses.definition: The collective body of judges, justices, etc.
The court system, inclusive of clerical staff, etc.
Judicial.

core.definition: The branch of government made up of courts and judges that interprets and applies the law.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'DISH'. The last syllables are weak, with 'air-ee' sounding like the word 'airy' pronounced with a rhotic r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and formal. It sounds institutional and is used in news, civics, and law.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use judiciary when talking about the court system as a whole, especially in civics and news: 'The judiciary is one of three branches of government.' In everyday conversation people usually say 'the courts' or 'the judges'. The word appears often with 'federal' or 'state' before it.

distinctions.note: A court is a single tribunal or building; the judiciary is the whole system of courts and judges.
Judicial is the adjective, meaning relating to courts; judiciary is the noun for the system.

examples.everyday: I just saw a news story about the federal judiciary, and I never really understood how judges get appointed.
examples.professional: The compliance team needs to coordinate with the state judiciary on the new data retention rules.
examples.analytical: A genuinely independent judiciary is essential to constitutional democracy, since it checks the executive and legislative branches.

nuance.analogy: The judiciary is like the referee's entire crew: the whole body that makes sure the rules are applied fairly.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin judiciarius, relating to judgment, from judicium, judgment.
common_mistakes: Using judiciary for a single court; it refers to the whole system.
Confusing judiciary with judicial, which is the adjective form.

senses.definition: A literal or metaphorical force or object regarded as unstoppable, that will crush all in its path.
An institution that incites destructive devotion or to which people are carelessly sacrificed.

core.definition: A massive, unstoppable force or organization that crushes everything in its path, or an institution people devote themselves to destructively.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, JUG. The second syllable is a weak 'er' and the last is 'nawt', rhymes with 'caught'. Do not pronounce it with a hard 'g' sound before 'er'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests overwhelming power, often with the sense of crushing people or ideas.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'juggernaut' for a company, product, team or movement that dominates its field, such as 'the Hollywood juggernaut.' It can be admiring or critical, depending on context. It is more common in media and conversation than in formal writing.

distinctions.note: 'Behemoth' stresses huge size; 'juggernaut' stresses unstoppable momentum and the power to crush.
'Powerhouse' is usually positive and describes strength or success; 'juggernaut' often implies something that flattens competitors or people.

examples.everyday: Their team is a juggernaut this season, and nobody in the league can beat them.
examples.professional: Our biggest competitor is a juggernaut in cloud storage, so we need a sharper niche.
examples.analytical: Institutions can become juggernauts that demand loyalty so complete that individuals are sacrificed to their momentum.

nuance.analogy: Like a giant truck on a downhill slope that cannot stop and flattens everything on the road.
nuance.etymology: From Hindi Jagannath, 'lord of the world,' a name of Krishna whose temple chariot at Puri was said to crush devotees under its wheels.
common_mistakes: Using it for a small, weak company, which contradicts its meaning of overwhelming power.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'jug-ER-naut'.
Spelling it 'juggernought' by analogy with 'naught'.

juggernaut.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century into British English in India, either through *جَگَنَّاتھ* / *जगन्नाथ* or directly from *ଜଗନ୍ନାଥ*, ultimately from Sanskrit *ज॒ग॒न्ना॒थ* (“lord of universe”), a title for the Hindu deity Vishnu's avatar Krishna.

senses.definition: A function used to define an integral transform.
senses.example: The Dirichlet kernel convolved with a function yields its Fourier series approximation.

senses.definition: The set of pairs of elements in the domain of f which are mapped to the same value; the equivalence relation x≡y⟺f(x)=f(y).
senses.example: If a function is continuous then its kernel is a closed set.

senses.definition: The set of elements of the domain of f which are mapped to an identity element.
The set of elements of G which are mapped to the identity of H (usually written as 0 in an additive group and as 1 in a multiplicative group).
The set of elements of R which are mapped to the additive identity 0 of S.
The set of elements of M which are mapped to the additive identity 0 of N.
The equalizer of f and the zero morphism from X to Y, denoted ker⁡f.
The set of members of a fuzzy set that are fully included (i.e. whose grade of membership is 1).
The core, center, or essence of an object or system.
senses.example: the kernel of an argument

senses.definition: A small mass around which other matter is concreted; a nucleus; a concretion or hard lump in the flesh.
The central part of many computer operating systems which manages the system's resources and the communication between hardware and software components.
senses.example: The Linux kernel is open-source.

senses.definition: The core engine of any complex software system.
The simplified input to an algorithm that has undergone kernelization.
The source of ker⁡f, denoted Ker⁡f.
The human clitoris.

A seed, metaphorically: a concept or principle with a distinct essence that exists within a larger context and has potential for growth, development, and propagation, by the same mental model as a seed of doubt or a kernel of truth (grain of truth), and comparable to a nugget (of wisdom, advice, etc) or a pearl (such as a pearl of wisdom).
Synonym of seedling (“plant variety from seedling origin”).
senses.example: Ashmead's Kernel

senses.definition: The central (usually edible) part of a nut, especially once the hard shell has been removed.
A single seed of grain, especially of corn or wheat.
The stone of certain fruits, such as peaches or plums.
The nucleus and electrons of an atom excluding its valence electrons.
To enclose within a kernel.
To crenellate.

core.definition: The soft inner part of a nut or seed, or the most important part of something (a kernel of truth); in computing, the core of an operating system; in machine learning and statistics, a function that measures the similarity of two inputs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The r is rhotic and the final syllable is a syllabic l, so do not add an extra vowel before the l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Among data scientists and statisticians, kernel is a standard technical term used in kernel density estimation and kernel methods. In ordinary American speech, people use kernel for the inner seed of a nut or grain, or for the core idea of something. In software, kernel refers to the core of an operating system.

distinctions.note: Core is a general word for the central part of something, while kernel in math refers to a specific function or set.
Seed is a biological or botanical word, while kernel in data science is a mathematical function.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the kernel in our model makes the data easier to separate, and I had no idea what she meant.
examples.professional: For the classifier, we selected a Gaussian kernel and tuned its bandwidth on the validation set.
examples.analytical: A positive definite kernel corresponds, by the Moore-Aronszajn theorem, to a unique reproducing kernel Hilbert space, which explains why kernel methods are so powerful.

nuance.analogy: A kernel is like a translator who measures how similar two sentences are in meaning without writing out a full translation of each one.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cyrnel, a diminutive of corn, meaning a small grain or seed.
common_mistakes: Confusing the machine learning kernel with the operating-system kernel, which are different senses of the same word.
Thinking a kernel is always a specific function, when it is a general category of similarity functions.

kernel.etymology: From Middle English *kernel*, *kirnel*, *kurnel*, from Old English *cyrnel*, from **kurnil*, diminutive of Proto-Germanic **kurną* (“seed, grain, corn”), equivalent to *corn* + *-le*.

senses.definition: To rest on one's bent knees, sometimes only one; to move to such a position.
To sink down so that the entrance is level with the pavement, making it easier for passengers to enter.
To cause to kneel.
senses.example: She knelt the doll to fit it into the box.

core.definition: To lower your body so your knees touch the ground, especially to pray, show respect, or work close to the floor.

pronunciation.tip: The k is silent: say NEEL. The vowel is a long 'ee', and the l is dark at the end of the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest humility, reverence, or submission depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: The past tense is knelt or kneeled; Americans use both, and kneeled is quite common. It is used in church, in proposals, and in practical tasks like gardening. Kneel down is natural, and kneel before someone suggests reverence or submission.

distinctions.note: Bow bends the head or upper body; kneel lowers the knees to the ground.
Crouch means bending low with knees up and weight on the feet; kneel puts knees on the ground.
Genuflect is a formal act of touching one knee to the ground in reverence, mostly in Catholic practice.

examples.everyday: I had to kneel down to reach the stuff under the sink.
examples.professional: Please kneel on the pad when you inspect the lower panel.
examples.analytical: In Philippians 2, the image of every knee bowing frames worship as acknowledgment of Christ's lordship.

nuance.etymology: From Old English cneowlian, from cneow, 'knee'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the silent k.
Using only 'knelt' as if 'kneeled' were wrong.
Saying 'kneel on the knees' instead of 'kneel' or 'kneel on one knee'.
nuance.biblical_note: Kneeling expresses worship, prayer, or submission. In 1 Kings 8:54, Solomon rises from kneeling before the altar after praying. In Daniel 6:10, Daniel kneels in prayer three times a day. In Philippians 2:10, every knee will bow at the name of Jesus; the Greek verb kampto means 'to bend.'

kneel.etymology: From Middle English *knelen*, from Old English *cnēowlian* (“to kneel”), equivalent to *knee* + *le*.

senses.definition: A break between stages of a journey.
senses.example: We had a layover while waiting to change planes, so we stretched our legs.

core.definition: A stop of several hours between connecting flights, or a break in the middle of a longer trip.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and 'over' is reduced to 'oh-ver' with a weak final syllable. Don't say 'lay-OH-ver' with stress on the second part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound tiring or inconvenient, but it is a routine part of air travel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'layover' for a stop between connecting flights, often in a hub airport like Chicago or Atlanta. A longer planned stop where you leave the airport is called a 'stopover.' A common phrase is 'I have a three-hour layover in Denver.'

distinctions.note: A stopover is usually a longer planned break where you may leave the airport and explore the city, while a layover is typically a shorter connection.
A connecting flight is the next flight itself, while the layover is the waiting time between flights.

examples.everyday: I have a four-hour layover in Denver, so I might grab lunch and catch up on emails.
examples.professional: The travel agency rebooked me on a flight with a shorter layover so I can still make the afternoon meeting.
examples.analytical: Airline networks often trade a longer layover for lower fares, which shifts inconvenience from the price to the passenger's time.

nuance.analogy: Like a pit stop in a race, where the car stops briefly before continuing toward the finish.
nuance.etymology: From the verb phrase 'lay over,' meaning to stop over or remain for a time before continuing a journey.
common_mistakes: Using 'stopover' and 'layover' interchangeably, when a stopover is usually longer and more deliberate.
Writing it as two words, 'lay over,' when it is used as a noun.

conversation.text: I have a three-hour layover in Denver.
We had a long layover, so we left the airport and got lunch.
I booked the cheaper flight, but it has two layovers.

senses.definition: Any of a variety of computing techniques that delay the computation of expressions until (and unless) the results are needed.

core.definition: A programming strategy that delays computing an expression until its result is actually needed, and then computes it only once.

pronunciation.tip: 'Lazy' takes stress on 'LAY,' and 'evaluation' shifts its stress to 'AY,' unlike the verb 'EV-uh-wayt' with stress on the first syllable. Keep the vowels in the middle weak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. The word 'lazy' is a term of art here, not an insult about the programmer.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers in the United States use 'lazy evaluation' as a standard term in functional programming, especially in Haskell. The word 'lazy' describes the strategy, not a careless programmer. In casual talk, developers may say 'Haskell is lazy by default.'

distinctions.note: Eager evaluation computes an expression as soon as it is encountered, while lazy evaluation waits until the value is needed.
Memoization caches the result of a computation so it is not repeated, while lazy evaluation defers the computation itself, and the two often work together.

examples.everyday: My brother who codes says his Haskell program uses lazy evaluation, so it doesn't calculate things until he asks for them.
examples.professional: We can use lazy evaluation in the data pipeline so we don't load every record before the report actually needs it.
examples.analytical: Lazy evaluation separates the description of a computation from its execution, which allows programs to define infinite structures without exhausting memory.

nuance.analogy: Like ordering food only when you are hungry, rather than cooking the whole menu in advance.
common_mistakes: Thinking 'lazy' means slow or careless, when it refers to delaying computation until needed.
Confusing lazy evaluation with eager evaluation, which does the opposite.

senses.definition: Record a phone message in someone's voicemail.

core.definition: To record a spoken message in someone's voicemail box after they do not answer their phone.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on VOICE and secondary stress on MAIL, so do not stress the second word equally. The 'a' is a weak schwa, so say 'leev-uh' quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a routine, everyday phrase for phone communication.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'leave a voicemail' for calls to cell phones and office lines when the person does not pick up. Friendly invitations include 'Feel free to leave a voicemail.' If someone asks 'Did you leave a voicemail?', a natural answer is 'Yes, I left one this morning.'

distinctions.note: Leave a message is the broader phrase and can refer to a note or a message passed through another person, while voicemail means audio recorded on the phone system.
A text is a written message sent from one phone to another, while a voicemail is spoken and stored for the recipient to play back.

examples.everyday: I called you twice, so just leave a voicemail and I'll call back after dinner.
examples.professional: I left a voicemail for the client about the contract, so please follow up if she doesn't reply by Friday.
examples.analytical: Leaving a voicemail is an asynchronous act, so the speaker must anticipate how the message will be received without the cues of a live conversation.

nuance.analogy: Like leaving a recorded note on a door, which the owner plays back later.
nuance.etymology: A compound of 'voice' (from Latin vox) and 'mail' (from Old French male, 'bag'), describing spoken messages stored for later delivery.
common_mistakes: Saying 'put a voicemail' instead of 'leave a voicemail'.
Stressing MAIL as strongly as VOICE; the first syllable of voicemail carries the main stress.

conversation.text: I left a voicemail, but she hasn't called back.
Don't leave a voicemail; nobody listens to them anymore. Just text.
If I don't answer, leave a voicemail, and I'll call you back.

senses.definition: A narrow surface projecting horizontally from a wall, cliff, or other surface.
A shelf on which articles may be laid.
A layer or stratum.
A lode; a limited mass of rock bearing valuable mineral.
A piece of timber to support the deck, placed athwartship between beams.
A provincial or territorial legislature building.
A provincial or territorial legislative assembly.
A shelf, ridge, or reef, of rocks.
A (door or window) lintel.
A cornice.
(uncommon) To cause to have, or to develop, a ledge (during mining, canal construction, building, etc).
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: A narrow, flat surface that sticks out horizontally from a wall, cliff, or other vertical surface.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single syllable with a short e and the soft j sound at the end. Don't add a vowel after the d; the consonant cluster is quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a plain descriptive word for physical structures.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ledge for a window ledge, a mountain ledge, or a ledge on a building. It is a neutral everyday word, and it often appears in warnings or practical descriptions. You might hear someone say the cat jumped up onto the window ledge, or be careful, there is a ledge up ahead.

distinctions.note: A shelf is usually a separate piece of furniture or a built-in board for holding objects, while a ledge is a projecting part of a wall, cliff, or building.
An edge is any border or boundary of a surface, while a ledge is a horizontal projecting surface, often a place where one can stand or sit.

examples.everyday: Put the plant on the window ledge so it gets some sun.
examples.professional: The contractor said the old brick wall needs a new concrete ledge to support the balcony.
examples.analytical: The altar described in Ezekiel is built in stepped tiers, and each tier narrows into a ledge that defines its height and proportion.

nuance.analogy: A ledge is like a step that sticks out from a wall instead of going up a staircase.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English ledge, probably related to lay, 'to lay down'.
common_mistakes: Confusing ledge with edge: a ledge is a projecting surface, not just a border.
Using shelf for a stone outcrop on a mountain, where ledge is the natural word.
nuance.biblical_note: The word ledge appears in the RSV description of the altar in Ezekiel 43. In Ezekiel 43:13-17 the altar is described as built in tiers, with a ledge at each level and a surrounding rim. The passage uses the ledges to show the structure's dimensions and the exact measurements of the altar.

ledge.etymology: From Middle English *legge*, from Old English *leċġ* (“bar, crossbeam”), from **laggju* (“layer, strip, ledge, rung, bar”), from Proto-Germanic **lagjō* (“layer, stratum”), from Proto-Indo-European **legʰ-* (“to lie, recline”).

let-me-read-that-back-to-you.phonetic: /ˌlɛt mi ˌɹɛd ðæt ˈbæk tu ju/

senses.definition: Repeating information to confirm it's correct.

core.definition: I'll repeat the information to you so we can confirm it's correct.

pronunciation.respelling: let mee red that BAK too yoo
pronunciation.tip: 'To you' reduces to 'tuh yuh' or 'chuh-yuh' in fast speech. Keep 'read' as the past form, 'red', and stress 'back'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and courteous. It signals that you care about getting details right.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the full version to make the other person feel included, especially on a phone call or in a customer service exchange. The shorter form 'let me read that back' is more common among colleagues. A natural reply is 'Yes, that's correct' or 'Yes, that's right.'

distinctions.note: 'Repeat' just says it again. 'Read back' often means reading from notes you wrote down, to confirm the details.
'Confirm' names the purpose. 'Read back to you' is the method.

collocations: let me read that back to you
read the details back to you
read back the address to you

examples.everyday: You want the blue one in medium, delivered Thursday? Let me read that back to you so there's no mix-up.
examples.professional: Let me read that back to you: the server migration starts Monday, and the rollback window is four hours.
examples.analytical: In a formal exchange, reading back is a verification protocol, and it shifts responsibility for accuracy onto both speakers.

nuance.analogy: Like a pilot repeating air traffic control instructions: the repetition catches errors before they matter.
nuance.etymology: 'Read' from Old English rædan; 'back' from Old English bæc; 'to you' from Old English to plus the pronoun.
common_mistakes: Saying 'read back you' instead of 'read that back to you'.
Using 'read' in the present sense; here it is pronounced 'red'.

conversation.text: Let me read that back to you: one large pizza, extra cheese.
OK, let me read that back to you to make sure I have it right.
"My number is 555-0186." "Let me read that back to you: 555-0186."

senses.definition: The branch of mathematics that deals with vectors, vector spaces, linear transformations and systems of linear equations.
An associative algebra.

core.definition: The branch of mathematics that studies vectors, vector spaces, linear transformations, and systems of linear equations.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on AL in the second word, and the first word has a light secondary stress on LIN-ee-er. The final -er in "linear" is a reduced r-colored vowel, and the -bra at the end is a quick schwa-like sound, so say AL-juh-bruh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "linear algebra" in university courses, data science, engineering, and machine learning. It is the standard name in the United States, and people rarely shorten it. Outside technical settings, it is seldom mentioned in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: "Algebra" is the broad field of symbols and operations, while "linear algebra" focuses specifically on linear structures such as vector spaces and matrices.
Matrix algebra is a practical part of linear algebra, while linear algebra also covers abstract vector spaces and transformations.

examples.everyday: My son is taking linear algebra this semester, and he says it's harder than calculus.
examples.professional: Our recommendation model depends on linear algebra, so the team reviews matrix factorization before each release.
examples.analytical: Much of quantum mechanics is built on the framework of linear algebra, especially on Hilbert spaces and operators.

nuance.analogy: Linear algebra is the grammar of vectors: it tells you how arrows can combine, stretch, and rotate in a consistent way.
nuance.etymology: "Linear" comes from Latin linearis, from linea, line; "algebra" comes from Arabic al-jabr, the reunion of broken parts.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable in "algebra" by saying al-JEE-bruh.
Confusing "linear algebra" with "elementary algebra," which is a broader and more basic subject.

senses.definition: The stage of the Atkinson–Shiffrin memory model where informative knowledge is held indefinitely.

core.definition: In cognitive models and AI, the storage stage that holds information for an extended period, sometimes indefinitely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MEM in 'memory'. The 'er' in 'term' is an American r-colored vowel, and the final 'y' in 'memory' is a light 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: In American psychology courses, long-term memory is standard, and in AI discussions it often refers to an analogy with human memory: 'the agent needs long-term memory to store user preferences.' In everyday talk, people say 'I have a good long-term memory' or 'I remember it from long ago.' The hyphenated form is common in writing when it modifies a noun.

distinctions.note: Short-term memory holds information for seconds to minutes, while long-term memory keeps it for much longer.
Working memory is the active workspace where you manipulate information, while long-term memory is the storage it draws from.

examples.everyday: My grandmother can't remember what she ate today, but she recalls her childhood songs, so her long-term memory is still strong.
examples.professional: The agent should write the user's preferences into long-term memory so it doesn't have to ask again next week.
examples.analytical: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model distinguishes long-term memory from sensory and short-term stores, but the boundary between them remains empirically contested.

nuance.analogy: Long-term memory is like a library: items are shelved and kept for years, and you go there to find them when you need them.
nuance.etymology: From long, term (a period of time), and memory, from Latin memoria.
common_mistakes: Writing 'long term memory' without a hyphen when it modifies a noun; the hyphen is standard in writing.
Confusing 'long-term' with 'long time': 'long-term plan' means over years, not just a long wait.

conversation.text: Long-term memory lets the assistant remember user preferences across sessions, usually by saving notes to a database.
If we add long-term memory, users need a way to see and delete what's stored.
In humans, long-term memory can hold information for years, unlike short-term memory.

senses.definition: The quality of being long-lasting, especially of life.
senses.example: Grandpa had incredible longevity: he lived to be 105 years old!

senses.definition: Duration over time; persistence.

core.definition: The length of time a person, animal, product or thing lasts or lives; how long something stays healthy or in use.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, JEH, and the final -ity is a reduced 'tee' sound, not 'ih-tee'. Americans pronounce the first vowel as 'ah' because of the cot-caught merger.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It usually praises a long, healthy life or a durable product, though it can be neutral when discussing statistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use longevity mostly when talking about how long people live, such as in health news or a retirement conversation. In casual speech they more often say 'how long someone lived' or 'lives to be 100.' For products or businesses, longevity means lasting well over many years.

distinctions.note: Lifespan is the typical or maximum length of life for a species; longevity is the quality of living long, often in an individual or group.
Durability describes how well a physical object resists wear; longevity can describe people, careers or ideas as well as objects.

examples.everyday: My grandmother lived to 98, so everyone in the family credits her longevity to good soup and daily walks.
examples.professional: The product team tested the battery under heat and cold to confirm its longevity before we promised a five-year warranty.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the longevity of ancient empires reflects institutional strength or simply the accidents of geography.

nuance.analogy: Longevity is like a well-built old house that keeps standing for generations because it was made to last.
nuance.etymology: From Latin longaevus, 'long-lived,' from longus 'long' and aevum 'age.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as 'long' with an 'aw' sound; it is closer to 'lahn.'
Using longevity for a single short event instead of a long period.

senses.definition: Lose a skill or ability you used to have.

core.definition: To stop being as good at something you used to do well, such as a skill, talent, or ability.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TOUCH, with a light secondary stress on lose. Your is reduced, and the ch in touch is a single voiceless sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to light and humorous; it can be used about yourself jokingly or about others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say lose your touch with a friendly, sometimes joking tone, often about cooking, sports, or a hobby. It is mostly used in casual speech and writing. A natural reply is Maybe I'm losing my touch, or No, you haven't lost your touch at all.

distinctions.note: Get rusty means your skill has weakened from lack of practice, while lose your touch suggests a loss of natural ability or flair.
Lose it is about losing control of emotions or your mind, not about losing a skill.

collocations: lose your touch on the court
lose your touch with the crowd

examples.everyday: My grandmother's pie is still perfect, so she hasn't lost her touch at all.
examples.professional: I think I have lost my touch with spreadsheets since I started managing the team.
examples.analytical: Some critics argue that the composer lost his touch once his style became more predictable.

nuance.analogy: Like an athlete who used to make every shot, losing your touch means the skill is still there but no longer works as well.
common_mistakes: Saying lost your touch when the sentence needs a present perfect form such as have lost your touch.
Confusing touch with feel in the sense of skill.

conversation.text: You haven't lost your touch; that pie is amazing.
I missed every shot tonight. I think I'm losing my touch.
Don't worry, you won't lose your touch after a few weeks off.

senses.definition: Unexpected help; miracle, deus ex machina, godsend.

core.definition: An unexpected piece of good luck or help that arrives exactly when you need it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAN-uh more lightly than on HEV-un; heaven is the main stress. Say frum with a reduced vowel, and link the phrase smoothly as man-uh-frum.

nuance.connotation: Positive, often warm and a bit humorous; it suggests gratitude for a welcome surprise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say manna from heaven when a sudden help or payment comes at the right moment, such as a last-minute ride or a canceled meeting that frees an afternoon. A natural reply is Oh, that's great, I'm so glad it worked out, or Wow, lucky you. Do not use it for everyday purchases or ordinary chores.

distinctions.note: Godsend is a near-synonym that emphasizes something very welcome; manna from heaven is more playful and biblical in its image.
A stroke of luck is simply good fortune; manna from heaven suggests help that feels almost miraculous.

examples.everyday: When my neighbor offered to watch the kids for the evening, it was manna from heaven.
examples.professional: The client's early payment was manna from heaven, because our cash flow had been very tight.
examples.analytical: Some theologians read providence in every stroke of luck, but calling a timely gift manna from heaven sharpens the question of how we recognize grace.

nuance.analogy: Manna from heaven is like finding a twenty-dollar bill in your coat pocket on a day when you thought you had no money left.
nuance.etymology: Combines manna (Hebrew man, what is it?) with heaven, from Old English heofon.
common_mistakes: Using the phrase for ordinary, expected help, which sounds exaggerated.
Stressing manna as heavily as heaven in speech; the stress falls mainly on heaven.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase comes from the story of the manna that God provided in the wilderness, described in Exodus 16. Its everyday use transfers the image of unexpected provision to any timely help.

manna-from-heaven.etymology: Referencing the miraculous food described in the Bible (Exodus 16:4–36).

senses.definition: Resembling marble or a marble statue; cold, smooth, white, etc. marblelike.

core.definition: Resembling marble; cold, smooth, white, and polished like a marble statue.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MOR, and the r is pronounced clearly in both the first and second syllables. The final -eal sounds like 'ul', with the last syllable reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, suggesting coldness, stiffness or lifelessness, though it can also praise smooth, pale beauty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use marmoreal almost only in literary or art-critical writing, such as describing a face, skin or a building as smooth and white like marble. In conversation it would sound overly bookish, so say 'marble-like' or 'white as marble' instead. It is never used for ordinary objects.

distinctions.note: Marble-like is plain and everyday, while marmoreal is literary and more evocative.
Pallid stresses unhealthy paleness, whereas marmoreal stresses smoothness and classical stillness.

examples.everyday: Her face looked almost marmoreal in the flat winter light, so still I thought she was posing for a painting.
examples.professional: The museum brochure described the sculpture's marmoreal surface, though the restorers noted it was actually limestone.
examples.analytical: Keats's urn stands in a marmoreal stillness that makes its figures eternal and also strangely remote from human life.

nuance.analogy: A marmoreal face is like a statue carved from marble: beautiful, smooth and cold to the touch.
nuance.etymology: From Latin marmoreus, 'of marble', from marmor, 'marble'.
common_mistakes: Using marmoreal for any white object instead of something truly marble-like.
Stressing the first syllable (MAR-mor-ee-al) instead of the second.

senses.definition: A piece of harness used on a horse to keep it from raising its head above a desired point.
A stochastic process for which the conditional expectation of future values given the sequence of all prior values is equal to the current value.
senses.example: If a gambler plays a fair game repeatedly, his payoff over time is a martingale.

senses.definition: A strategy in which one doubles the stake after each loss.
A strap attached to the sword handle, preventing a sword being dropped if disarmed.
A spar, or piece of rigging that strengthens the bowsprit.
To employ the martingale strategy in gambling.

core.definition: In probability, a random process whose expected next value, given all past values, equals its current value, so it has no predictable drift.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the r is pronounced clearly in American English. The final syllable rhymes with 'tale', not 'mile' or 'mail' with a stressed vowel shift.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Statisticians, quants and data scientists use this word in their professional work, usually in phrases like 'the price process is a martingale'. Outside those fields it is mostly heard in gambling, where the doubling strategy has the same name. Specify which sense you mean when talking to non-specialists.

distinctions.note: A random walk is a sum of independent steps, which is a martingale only when the steps have zero mean; a martingale only needs the conditional expectation condition, so it is more general.
A Markov chain's future depends only on its present state; a martingale's future expectation depends on its full history but is equal to its current value.

examples.everyday: My sister works at a hedge fund and says the stock price is basically a martingale, so today's price is the best guess for tomorrow.
examples.professional: Before we rely on the residual series for forecasting, we should test whether it behaves like a martingale difference sequence.
examples.analytical: A process is a martingale when the conditional expectation of its next value, given the entire history, equals its present value, which encodes the idea of a fair game.

nuance.analogy: A martingale is like a fair coin game where your best guess for your fortune tomorrow is exactly what you have today.
nuance.etymology: From French, of uncertain origin; the gambling sense comes from the harness, which was named for its supposed use by a Martin.
common_mistakes: Saying martingale for any random process; it requires the specific expected-value condition.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable, as in mar-TIN-gale.
patterns: a martingale with respect to sth

martingale.etymology: From Middle French *martingale*, from Occitan *martegalo*, feminine form of *martegal*, an inhabitant of Martigues, which is from Latin *maritima*.

senses.definition: Words and music written for a masque.
A masquerade.
A facial mask.
senses.example: mud masque; clay masque

core.definition: A courtly entertainment of music, dance, and drama, popular in 16th- and 17th-century England, often performed for a royal audience.

pronunciation.tip: Say it exactly like mask. The spelling with -que is silent, so the final sound is the k of mask and there is no extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a historical or literary term
nuance.usage_note: Americans use masque almost only in literary history, theater history, or discussions of Renaissance drama, such as Ben Jonson's court masques. In everyday speech they say mask for a face covering and masquerade for a costume party. The word may appear in a play program or museum label, but it sounds old-fashioned in casual talk.
word_family: masquer (noun, a performer in a masque)
masquing (noun, the practice of performing masques)

distinctions.note: A mask is a covering for the face, while a masque is a dramatic entertainment in which masks and costumes were often worn.
A masquerade is a party or a pretense, while a masque is a specific theatrical form with music and dance.

examples.everyday: The theater group is putting on a masque next spring, with singing, dancing, and elaborate costumes.
examples.professional: Her dissertation on Jonson's court masques shows how music and staging carried political messages to the Stuart court.
examples.analytical: Ben Jonson's masques combined spectacle and verse to flatter the monarchy while quietly negotiating its authority.

nuance.analogy: Like a grand historical pageant performed indoors, where the music and costumes carry the message as much as the words.
nuance.etymology: From French masque, from Italian maschera, 'mask.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the -que as an extra syllable, like mask-ay.
Using masque to mean a face covering, where mask is the normal American word.

senses.definition: Having little flesh; lean; thin.
Poor, deficient or inferior in amount, quality or extent.
senses.example: A meager piece of cake in one bite.

senses.definition: Of a set: such that, considered as a subset of a (usually larger) topological space, it is in a precise sense small or negligible.
Dry and harsh to the touch (e.g. as chalk).
To make lean.

core.definition: Very small or insufficient in amount or quality, especially much less than what is needed or expected.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the second syllable a reduced 'ur' sound, like 'er' in 'butter'. The American spelling 'meager' pairs with this pronunciation, while British 'meagre' is the other spelling.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'meager' to describe small or poor amounts, such as a meager salary, meager portions, or meager results. It has a clear negative tone, so use it to complain or describe a problem rather than to praise. In American spelling, it is written 'meager,' not 'meagre.'

distinctions.note: 'Scant' means barely enough or hardly any, while 'meager' emphasizes that something is small, poor or inadequate in quality or quantity.
'Sparse' describes things spread thinly, like trees or population, while 'meager' describes limited resources or results.

examples.everyday: The restaurant gave us a meager portion of rice for twenty dollars, so we went out for a snack afterward.
examples.professional: Our quarterly results were meager, so we need a clear plan to increase sales before the next board meeting.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the evidence is meager, and therefore cannot support the sweeping conclusion drawn in the final chapter.

nuance.analogy: A meager meal is like a bowl with only a few crumbs left in the bottom.
nuance.etymology: From Old French maigre, from Latin macer, meaning 'thin' or 'lean.'
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'meagre,' which is the British form.
Pronouncing it like 'mega,' with a long a sound.

meager.etymology: From Middle English *megre*, from Anglo-Norman *megre*, Old French *maigre*, from Latin *macer*, from Proto-Indo-European **mh₂ḱrós*.

senses.definition: The discipline which deals with the relationship of parts with their respective wholes.

core.definition: The branch of philosophy and logic that studies parts, wholes, and how parts make up a whole.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the middle syllable, -RAH-. Americans reduce the first syllable to a schwa, so start with a quick 'muh' rather than 'mer.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in philosophy and logic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mereology in academic philosophy, metaphysics, and logic courses, and in discussions of formal ontology. It is not a word for everyday conversation. If a non-specialist hears it, they may need an example, such as a car being more than its parts, to understand it.

distinctions.note: Ontology is the broader study of what exists, while mereology is the narrower study of parthood and wholeness.
Topology studies shape and continuity in mathematics, while mereology studies the relation of parts to wholes.
Set theory studies membership in collections, while mereology studies parts within a whole.

examples.everyday: I took a philosophy class where we talked about mereology, the idea that a whole is more than just its parts.
examples.professional: Our ontology team uses mereology to model how components belong to a larger system in the knowledge graph.
examples.analytical: Classical mereology argues that composition is governed by axioms about overlap and sums, which shapes how we answer questions about material objects.

nuance.analogy: Mereology is like studying a LEGO castle: it asks which bricks belong to the castle, how they fit together, and what counts as the whole.
nuance.etymology: From Greek meros, part, with the suffix -logy, the study of.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in MER-ee-ol-o-gy; the stress is on the -RAH- syllable.
Confusing mereology with ontology or mythology in conversation.
Using mereology to mean a single part of something; it names the field of study.

mereology.etymology: Coined by Stanisław Leśniewski in 1927, from Ancient Greek *μέρος* (“part”) *-logy*.

senses.definition: An originally Ancient Greek form of theater in which the audience participates and improvises.
The relation between a particular and a Platonic form.

core.definition: In Plato's philosophy, the relation by which a particular thing participates in or shares a quality of its Form.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, THEK. The th is voiceless as in 'think'. The final -is is a short 'iss' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term in philosophy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in academic philosophy, usually in courses on Plato or Neoplatonism. It is not a conversational word. In general discussion, you would simply say participation, which is its usual English equivalent in translations of Plato.

distinctions.note: Mimesis means imitation or representation, while methexis means the particular actually sharing in the reality of a Form.
Participation is the common English translation of methexis; the Greek term is used when a scholar wants to stress the Platonic technical sense.

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor used the word methexis, and I had to look it up in the dictionary.
examples.professional: In the research paper, we defined methexis as the relation through which sensible objects share in their Forms.
examples.analytical: Plato's account of methexis raises the problem of how one Form can be wholly present in many particulars without being divided.

nuance.analogy: Like a copy of a photograph that gets its image from the original, a particular gets its character from the Form it shares in.
nuance.etymology: From Greek methexis, 'sharing, participation', from metechein, 'to share in'.
common_mistakes: Confusing methexis with mimesis, which is imitation rather than participation.
Pronouncing the th as a 't' sound.

senses.definition: Migrating.
Roving; wandering; nomadic.
senses.example: migratory habits; a migratory life

senses.definition: Clipping of migratory bird.

core.definition: Relating to animals that move regularly from one region to another, often with the seasons.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MY, with a secondary stress on the -tor syllable. The middle syllable is reduced to 'gruh,' and the ending is 'tor-ee' with a clear r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term, mostly used in science and nature writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use migratory for birds, fish, and other animals, as in 'migratory birds.' For people, 'migrant' is the normal word. Applied to people, migratory sounds technical or literary.

distinctions.note: Nomadic describes people or groups without permanent homes, while migratory describes regular movement that often returns to the same places.
Itinerant describes someone who travels from place to place for work, such as a preacher, while migratory describes regular seasonal movement.

examples.everyday: We love watching the migratory ducks land on the lake each November.
examples.professional: The park service tracks migratory species to plan the trail closures.
examples.analytical: The author describes the migratory culture of early settlers, who moved with the seasons.

nuance.analogy: Like a snowbird who spends the winter in Florida and returns north each spring.
nuance.etymology: From Latin migrare, to move from one place to another, plus the suffix -ory.
common_mistakes: Using 'migratory' for people; the usual word is 'migrant.'
Stressing the last syllable instead of MY.

senses.definition: An accident, mistake, or problem.
senses.example: Since the mishap with the banana peel, he watches his step.

senses.definition: Ill luck; misfortune; mischance.

core.definition: A minor accident or unlucky event that causes small trouble, delay, or embarrassment, but usually not serious harm.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MIS, and the second syllable is a short 'hap' rhyming with 'cap'. The 'sh' is a single sound, so do not add an extra vowel between the 's' and 'h'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative and light. It suggests an unlucky accident, not a disaster, so it can be used with some humor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word when something went wrong in a small way, such as spilling coffee or missing a train. It is common in casual speech and in polite apologies at work. For serious accidents, people say 'accident' or 'disaster' instead. A natural reply is 'No worries, these things happen'.

distinctions.note: Accident can describe any unplanned event, including serious ones; mishap usually describes a minor, mildly unlucky event.
Disaster is a major catastrophe; mishap is small and easily fixed.

examples.everyday: Sorry I am late, I had a little mishap with my coffee on the way to the office.
examples.professional: The presentation went smoothly apart from one mishap when the projector stopped working, but we recovered quickly.
examples.analytical: The historian treats the failed expedition not as a mere mishap but as a symptom of systemic overconfidence.

nuance.analogy: A mishap is like a small pebble on the road: it trips you for a moment, but it does not stop the journey.
nuance.etymology: From 'mis-' meaning badly plus 'hap', meaning chance or luck, from Middle English 'hap'.
common_mistakes: Using 'mishap' for serious accidents; for a car crash with injuries, say 'accident'.
Pronouncing 'mishap' with stress on the second syllable; the stress is on the first syllable, MIS.

core.definition: A person from Moab, the ancient kingdom east of the Dead Sea, and a descendant of Lot.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOH, and reduce the middle vowel to a quick 'uh.' The final syllable rhymes with 'kite.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most contexts. In Bible study, it can carry a sense of an outsider or a historic enemy of Israel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Moabite' mostly in Bible study, sermons and religious history. In everyday talk, it rarely comes up except when someone mentions Ruth. Capitalize it, and use it as a noun for a person or an adjective for things from Moab, such as 'Moabite pottery.'

distinctions.note: An Ammonite is a person from Ammon, another neighboring kingdom; the two peoples were often mentioned together in the Old Testament.
'Moabite' usually refers to one person, while 'Moabites' is the plural for the people as a whole.

examples.everyday: Ruth is called a Moabite in the Bible, which surprised me when I first read it.
examples.professional: The museum's exhibit includes a Moabite pottery bowl from the ninth century BC.
examples.analytical: Ruth the Moabite is a striking figure, because her loyalty to Naomi places a foreigner within the lineage of David.

nuance.analogy: Calling someone a Moabite in the Bible is like saying someone is from a neighboring country: it names their homeland and their people.
nuance.etymology: From Moab, with the suffix '-ite' meaning 'a member of' or 'a person from.'
common_mistakes: Using a lowercase 'm' for the proper adjective or noun.
Using 'Moabite' for the land itself; the land is Moab.
nuance.biblical_note: Moabite describes a member of the people of Moab. Ruth 1:4 names Moabite women as wives of Elimelech's sons, and Ruth 4:13-17 traces David's ancestry through Ruth the Moabite. Deuteronomy 23:3 excludes Moabites from the assembly of the Lord, and Judges 3:12-30 describes King Eglon of Moab oppressing Israel.

senses.definition: To create a mockup or prototype of.
To mimic, to simulate.
To make fun of, especially by mimicking; to taunt.
To tantalize, and disappoint the hopes of.
senses.example: The wind is mocking my efforts to light a fire!

senses.definition: (rare) To create an artistic representation of.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: An imitation, usually of lesser quality.
Mockery; the act of mocking.
Ellipsis of mock examination.
senses.example: He got a B in his History mock, but improved to an A in the exam.

senses.definition: A mockup or prototype; particularly, ellipsis of mock object, as used in unit testing.
Imitation, not genuine; fake.
senses.example: mock leather

core.definition: To imitate someone in a scornful or playful way, or in software testing, to replace a real component with a simulated stand-in.

pronunciation.tip: Rhymes with 'lock' and 'rock'; the vowel is the open American 'ah' (cot-caught merger). The final k is unreleased in fast speech, so it sounds almost like 'mah'.

nuance.connotation: Negative when used to ridicule someone; neutral in technical contexts such as 'mock the database' or 'mock the API'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mock' most often to mean making fun of someone by imitating them, as in 'Don't mock him, he's trying.' In tech, developers say they 'mock' a dependency during testing, which is a neutral, everyday term on engineering teams. As a noun, 'a mock' is a practice exam or a simulated trial, as in 'a mock interview.'

distinctions.note: 'Imitate' is neutral and may be admiring; 'mock' implies the imitation is meant to ridicule.
'Tease' is gentler and often affectionate; 'mock' is sharper and more clearly contemptuous.
'Simulate' is the neutral technical term for reproducing behavior; 'mock' in software usually means a small fake object used in tests.

examples.everyday: My brother always mocks my accent when I order coffee.
examples.professional: We'll mock the payment service so the integration tests don't hit the real vendor.
examples.analytical: Plato suggests that the poet can only mock the truth, offering a copy of a copy.

nuance.analogy: A mock is like a stunt double: it stands in for the real thing so you can test everything around it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle French 'mocquer', of uncertain origin, possibly from Middle Dutch 'mocken'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'mock at someone'; the standard form is 'mock someone' with no preposition.
Confusing 'mock' (verb or adjective) with 'mocking' in noun contexts; 'a mock' is a practice or simulated event.

mock.etymology: From Middle English *mokken*, from Old French *mocquer*, *moquier* (“to deride, jeer”), from Middle Dutch *mocken* (“to mumble”) or *mucken* (“to grumble, talk with the mouth half-opened”), both from **mokkijan*, **mukkijan* (“to low, bellow; mumble”),…

senses.definition: To make moist or moister.
senses.example: She put on some lip balm to moisten her lips.

senses.definition: To become moist or moister.
senses.example: His eyes began to moisten as he held back tears.

core.definition: To make something slightly wet, or to become slightly wet. Often used for food or for dry skin, lips, or cloth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is reduced and sounds like "sun" or "suhn." The "t" is silent, so do not pronounce it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds slightly more polished than "wet" and is often used for cooking or care instructions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "moisten" in recipes, cooking instructions, and descriptions of gentle wetting, such as moistening a cloth. In casual talk, people often say "wet" or "dampen" instead. The word is fine in both written and spoken American English.

distinctions.note: "Dampen" means to make something a little wet, often with the sense of lightly sprinkling. "Moisten" is more common in cooking and skin care.
"Wet" is the everyday, general word for covering something with liquid. "Moisten" means adding only a small amount.

examples.everyday: Moisten the paper towel a little before you wipe the counter.
examples.professional: Moisten the dough with a small amount of water until it holds together without sticking to your hands.
examples.analytical: The author describes the dry field that the rain slowly moistens, a gentle image of grace restoring what had withered.

nuance.analogy: To moisten something is like lightly misting a houseplant: you add just enough water to make it damp without flooding it.
nuance.etymology: Formed from "moist" with the verb suffix "-en," meaning to make or become.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the "t" in "moisten," which is silent.
Confusing "moisten" with "moisturize," which usually refers to adding oil or cream to skin or hair.

senses.definition: A computer program or system composed of multiple interacting intelligent agents, capable of solving highly complex problems which are difficult or impossible for an individual agent or monolithic system to solve.

core.definition: A computer system made of several interacting intelligent agents that work together, or compete, to solve problems too complex for one agent alone.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on AY in agent, not on the end of the word, and the second syllable of system is reduced to a schwa. Keep multi light, with the first syllable stressed only slightly, and say the phrase in one smooth breath.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in AI research, robotics, and engineering talks, usually in a design review or paper. Outside those fields people might say a system of agents or simply a set of AI bots. Multi-agent is often written with a hyphen in technical writing and without one in some company documents.

distinctions.note: A single-agent system has one decision-making agent, so it does not face other learners or coordination problems.
A distributed system is a network of computers sharing work, while a multi-agent system focuses on autonomous agents that make their own decisions and may cooperate or compete.

examples.everyday: My friend builds robots for a warehouse, and she says their multi-agent system lets the machines avoid bumping into each other.
examples.professional: In the design review we agreed that the multi-agent system should share one scheduling model rather than let each agent plan alone.
examples.analytical: A multi-agent system raises philosophical questions about how collective intelligence emerges from the local decisions of autonomous agents.

nuance.analogy: A multi-agent system is like a soccer team: each player makes independent decisions, yet the team succeeds only when they coordinate well.
nuance.etymology: Multi- from Latin multus (many); agent from Latin agens (acting, doing); system from Greek systēma (organized whole).
common_mistakes: Placing the primary stress on system or on multi instead of on agent.
Writing multiagent without a hyphen in formal technical writing, which is less common in US papers.
Using agent to mean a human salesperson in technical contexts, when the word refers to a software entity.

conversation.text: In a multi-agent system, several agents with different roles coordinate or compete to complete a task.
A multi-agent system adds coordination overhead; one capable agent with good tools is often enough.
Multi-agent systems are hard to train because each agent's environment keeps changing as the others learn.

senses.definition: The design of software tests by making slightly modified versions (mutants) of the program being tested. The value of a test suite is measured by how many of the mutants fail its tests.

core.definition: A software testing method that makes small deliberate changes (mutants) to code and checks whether the tests catch them.

pronunciation.tip: TEST is the main stress in the phrase, while TAY keeps a weaker stress. Make the -tion syllable sound like shun, not shin.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers on American software teams use the term in code reviews, continuous integration discussions and quality debates. Non-engineers may not know it, so explain it as testing your tests. Do not confuse it with genetic mutation, though the word mutant is shared.

distinctions.note: Unit testing checks that code behaves as expected; mutation testing checks how good the unit tests are at catching faults.
Coverage measures which lines run during tests; mutation testing measures whether tests detect injected bugs, a stronger measure.

examples.everyday: My friend who builds apps mentioned mutation testing, but I had no idea what it meant.
examples.professional: Let's add mutation testing to the CI pipeline so we know whether our unit tests catch real bugs.
examples.analytical: Mutation testing reframes test quality as the fraction of injected faults a suite detects, not merely the code it executes.

nuance.analogy: Like a security team planting fake intruders to see whether the alarm actually goes off.
nuance.etymology: Named by analogy with genetic mutation: mutation from Latin mutatio, change, and testing from test.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with genetic mutation
Assuming high code coverage means the tests are strong

senses.definition: Of, or relating to mystics, mysticism or occult mysteries; mystical.
senses.example: a mystic dance

senses.definition: Mysterious and strange; arcane, obscure or enigmatic.
Someone who practices mysticism.

core.definition: A person who seeks direct, personal experience of God or ultimate reality through prayer, meditation, or contemplation, rather than through reasoning alone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MIS. The second syllable is short and unstressed. Do not add an extra syllable at the end, since the word has only two.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in religious contexts, and sometimes slightly negative when used for people claiming secret knowledge
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mystic for a person who has deep spiritual experiences or follows a contemplative path. In popular speech it can also describe someone with a vague interest in the supernatural, so the tone can shift. In church or academic talk, it is respectful. Describing a person as a mystic can suggest someone unusually devoted or someone who is not very practical.

distinctions.note: A psychic claims to perceive hidden information, while a mystic seeks union with God or ultimate reality.

examples.everyday: My aunt loves reading about old Christian mystics, especially Julian of Norwich.
examples.professional: Our church retreat leader is a mystic, so the sessions focus on silent prayer.
examples.analytical: Meister Eckhart is often described as a speculative mystic who sought an identity between the soul and God.

nuance.analogy: A mystic is like a person who does not just read a map of a city but walks inside it until they know the streets by heart.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin mysticus, from Greek mystikos, relating to secret rites, from mystēs, an initiate.
common_mistakes: Using mystic as an adjective in place of mystical, as in a mystic experience instead of a mystical experience.
Confusing mystic with psychic or occultist, which are different meanings.

mystic.etymology: From Old French *mistique*, from Latin *mysticus*, from Ancient Greek *μυστικός* (“secret, mystic”), from *μύστης* (“one who has been initiated”).

senses.definition: The collection of myths of a people, concerning the origin of the people, history, deities, ancestors and heroes.
A similar body of myths concerning an event, person or institution.
Pervasive elements of a fictional universe that resemble a mythological universe.
The set of misconceptions and false attitudes that are held about something and contribute to its perception.
The systematic collection and study of myths.

core.definition: A collection of myths belonging to a people, explaining their origins, history, gods, ancestors, and heroes, or a similar body of stories about a person or institution.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, THAH, in American English. The middle syllable is reduced to a quick uh, and the final -gy sounds like jee. The th is voiceless.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in academic and cultural contexts, sometimes slightly dismissive when used of beliefs seen as false
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mythology for ancient stories such as Greek or Norse myths, and in everyday speech for popular beliefs that are false. Saying that a belief is mythology can sound dismissive, so use it carefully when talking with someone who holds that belief. In college courses, mythology is a common subject.

distinctions.note: A myth is a single traditional story, while mythology is the whole body or system of such stories.
Folklore is broader and includes folk tales, customs, and sayings, while mythology focuses on stories about gods, origins, and heroes.

examples.everyday: My daughter is reading a book on Greek mythology for school, and she keeps telling me about Zeus.
examples.professional: The company's founding story has become a kind of mythology, but the actual data is much more complicated.
examples.analytical: Lévi-Strauss argued that mythology can be analyzed as a system of oppositions that organize social thought.

nuance.analogy: Mythology is like an old family album: each story explains where a people came from and who they are, even when the details are symbolic.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mythologia, from mythos, story, plus logos, word or account.
common_mistakes: Confusing mythology with myth, using the plural as if it were a single story.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying MITH-uh-lah-jee instead of mih-THAH-luh-jee.

mythology.etymology: First attested as Middle English in 1412.

senses.definition: Lack of sophistication, experience, judgment or worldliness; artlessness; gullibility; credulity.

core.definition: A lack of experience or judgment that makes someone trust others too easily or not see complicated realities.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the last syllable, TAY. The second syllable is a reduced 'uh' before the stressed syllable, and the word is often written without accents in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use naivete more often than naivety. It can describe charming innocence or a harmful lack of judgment, depending on context. In a workplace, saying someone shows naivete suggests they need to learn more before deciding.

distinctions.note: Innocence suggests moral purity or not being guilty, while naivete suggests a lack of practical experience or judgment.
Ignorance is a lack of knowledge in general, while naivete is a trusting lack of worldly awareness that can be charming or harmful.

examples.everyday: Her naivete about apartment rental scams made her trust the wrong landlord.
examples.professional: His naivete about the procurement process led him to approve a vendor without a proper review.
examples.analytical: The author treats the young theologian's naivete as a sign of sincerity rather than of intellectual weakness.

nuance.analogy: Naivete is like a clear window with no curtains: you see the world openly, but everyone else can also see in.
nuance.etymology: From French naïveté, from naïf, 'naive'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'teet' instead of 'tay'.
Using naivete as a countable noun, such as 'a naivete', when it is usually uncountable.

senses.definition: The state or characteristic of being nefarious.

core.definition: The quality of being wicked, criminal, or shamefully evil, especially in someone's plans or behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'fair', and the last syllables are reduced to 'us-nus'. Don't add an extra syllable at the end; it is four syllables after the stress.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative; it describes criminal or evil character, usually in formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'nefariousness' in speech; they usually say 'wickedness', 'evil intent', or simply describe the nefarious act. It appears mostly in journalism, legal or literary writing. It is correct but sounds heavy in casual talk.

distinctions.note: 'Wickedness' is a broader, more common word, while 'nefariousness' emphasizes criminal or secret plotting.
'Criminality' refers to crime itself, while 'nefariousness' includes the sense of evil intent behind it.

examples.professional: The auditor documented the nefariousness of the scheme, including forged invoices and hidden transfers.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the nefariousness of the regime lay less in its violence than in its systematic corruption of language.

nuance.analogy: Nefariousness is like a hidden crack in a bridge: you may not see it, but the whole structure is unsafe.
nuance.etymology: From 'nefarious' plus the suffix '-ness', meaning the state or quality of being nefarious.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle syllables, saying 'nef-air-ee-OUS-ness' instead of stressing the second syllable.
Using 'nefariousness' for ordinary bad behavior; it is best reserved for serious wrongdoing.

senses.definition: Your phone has no cell signal.

core.definition: A phrase shown on a phone meaning it has no cell signal, so calls and internet may not work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SUR in service, and the second syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'vus', not 'vees'. The r is strong in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it describes a technical problem rather than a human one.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see it on phone screens, especially when traveling, in basements, or in rural areas. People say 'I've got no service here' or 'I lost service.' It is common and informal, and it refers to signal, not to customer service.

distinctions.note: Customer service means help provided by a company; no service on a phone means no cell signal.
No signal is also common; no service is the phrase most Americans see on phone status bars.

examples.everyday: I can't call you back from the hike. I've got no service up here.
examples.professional: I'm in the parking garage, so I have no service and will rejoin the call in a few minutes.
examples.analytical: The message no service reveals how much modern work depends on an invisible network that we rarely notice until it fails.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio that goes silent when you drive into a tunnel.
common_mistakes: Using 'service' to mean a bad phone quality rather than the absence of signal.
Saying 'no signal' and 'no service' interchangeably in formal writing without considering the audience.

conversation.text: There's no service in this canyon, so we used a paper map.
My phone says "No Service" in the basement.
Sorry I didn't call back; I had no service at the cabin.

senses.definition: Not monotonic.

core.definition: In logic and AI, describing reasoning where adding new information can invalidate conclusions that were previously accepted.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the 'tah' syllable, and the 'o' in 'mon' and the second 'o' are both pronounced with the cot vowel. Learners often add an extra syllable or stress the first part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in formal logic, philosophy of AI and knowledge representation. It describes the everyday experience that new evidence can overturn a conclusion, as in 'the bird can fly' being withdrawn after learning it is a penguin. It is rarely used outside technical or academic talk.

distinctions.note: Monotonic means always moving in one direction, which in logic means conclusions are never retracted; nonmonotonic means conclusions can be retracted.
Defeasible describes a conclusion that can be overridden by exceptions; nonmonotonic describes the logical system or inference pattern that allows this.

examples.professional: The chatbot uses nonmonotonic reasoning, so it can revise its answer when a user supplies a new fact.
examples.analytical: A nonmonotonic logic permits a conclusion to be withdrawn when further premises are added, which marks a fundamental departure from classical deductive consequence.

nuance.analogy: Ordinary deduction is like a sealed box: once something is inside it stays there. Nonmonotonic reasoning is like a whiteboard where new evidence can erase a previous answer.
nuance.etymology: From non- (not) plus monotonic, from monotone, from Greek monotonos, single-toned.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'MON-uh-TAH-nik' or 'non-muh-NOT-ik'.
Using it to mean simply 'not monotone' in everyday speech about voices or music, where 'monotone' is the usual word.

senses.definition: A garden or an area of land for the cultivation of fruit or nut trees.
The trees themselves cultivated in such an area.

core.definition: A piece of land where fruit or nut trees are planted and cared for, such as an apple orchard or a cherry orchard.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ch is a plain ch sound, and the ending -ard is a reduced r-colored schwa plus d, so it is one syllable: OR-churd.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests countryside, harvest, and peaceful rural life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use orchard for a farm area of fruit trees, such as an apple or peach orchard, and many families visit them to pick fruit in the fall. A grove is more often used for citrus, and a vineyard is for grapes. Orchard is common and neutral in everyday talk, including weekend plans.
word_family: orchardist (noun, a person who grows fruit trees)

distinctions.note: An orchard is usually fruit or nut trees planted in rows; a grove often means citrus trees or a small group of trees.
A vineyard grows grapes for wine or eating; an orchard grows tree fruit.
A farm is broader and may include crops and animals; an orchard is a specific area of fruit trees.

examples.everyday: Let's drive out to the apple orchard on Saturday and pick some Honeycrisps.
examples.professional: The orchard supplier can deliver pears in bulk by the first week of September.
examples.analytical: Chekhov's The Cherry Orchard uses the orchard as a symbol of an old family losing its land and identity.

nuance.analogy: An orchard is like a row of friends who each bear fruit in their own season.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ortgeard, 'herb or vegetable garden', later applied to gardens of fruit trees.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable after the r; it is one syllable, OR-churd.
Using orchard for a forest or wild grove; an orchard is planted and tended.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word pardes, meaning an orchard or cultivated garden, appears in the Song of Songs, where the beloved's shoots are described as an orchard of pomegranates with precious fruits (Song of Songs 4:13). In Ecclesiastes 2:5 the Preacher describes planting gardens and orchards of every kind of fruit tree as part of his great works. The word pardes is the origin of the English word paradise, which carries the image of a well-tended garden.

orchard.etymology: From Middle English *orchard*, *orcherd*, from Old English *orċeard*, *ortġeard*, a compound of **ort* (probably from Proto-Germanic **urtiz*, a dissimilated variant of Proto-Germanic **wurt-* (“wort”), later incorrectly associated with unrelated ) +…

senses.definition: The ceremony in which a priest is consecrated, considered a sacrament in the Catholic and Orthodox churches.
The act of ordaining or the state of being ordained.
The ceremony in which a bhikkhu or bhikkhuni is ordained into the sangha.

A statistical technique for ordering data from a large number of sites or populations by arranging the data as points in a multidimensional coordinate frame, in which patterns can be discerned; an instance of this.

core.definition: The religious ceremony in which a person is formally made a priest, minister, or other church leader.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NAY, the third syllable. The -tion ending is pronounced shun, and the final n is a syllabic n, so there is no extra vowel before it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and solemn. It names a formal religious rite and carries respect in church contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ordination when talking about churches, pastors, rabbis, or the clergy. In casual speech people often say he was ordained or she got ordained. Be careful with the word ordination in a religious setting, as it can refer to a sacrament in some churches and a formal commissioning in others.

distinctions.note: Consecration is the setting apart of a person, object, or place for sacred use, and it is used especially for bishops and sacred objects, while ordination is the broader rite for clergy.
Installation is the formal placement of a pastor into a particular congregation, while ordination is the rite that gives someone the office itself.

examples.everyday: My friend is going to be ordained next month, and we are all going to her ordination service.
examples.professional: The diocese scheduled three ordinations for the summer, pending final background checks.
examples.analytical: The ordination of a priest confers a sacramental character that the church regards as permanent, which distinguishes it from a simple appointment to office.

nuance.analogy: Ordination is like a graduation ceremony for a profession, but within the church it also confers a special status.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ordinatio, arrangement or appointment, from ordinare, to put in order.
common_mistakes: Saying ordinate or ordinance when you mean ordination, which are different words with different meanings.
Using ordination for any church appointment; the term refers to the formal rite.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, the act of setting people apart for service is expressed by the Greek word cheirotonia, meaning appointment by the raising of hands, and by the laying on of hands (Greek epithesis ton cheiron). Acts 14:23 says Paul and Barnabas appointed elders in every church. 1 Timothy 4:14 speaks of the gift received through the laying on of hands by the council of elders. 2 Timothy 1:6 says Timothy should stir up the gift of God through Paul's laying on of hands.

traditions.view: Ordination is a sacrament, through which a bishop, priest, or deacon receives grace for ministry through the laying on of hands and prayer, and the rite is confined to the clergy.
Ordination is one of the seven sacraments, which confers an indelible character on bishops, priests, and deacons, and is reserved to baptized men.

Most Protestant churches see ordination as a church commissioning to ministry rather than a sacrament, though Lutherans and Anglicans have a more sacramental understanding, and Baptists and many others treat it as a recognition of calling.

ordination.etymology: From Middle French *ordination*, from Old French *ordinacion*, from Latin *ordinatio*.

senses.definition: One of the centers (UK:centers) of a triangle, defined as being the intersection of its three altitudes; in an acute triangle, it is inside the triangle; in an obtuse triangle, it is outside the triangle; in a right-angled triangle it is the vertex opposite the hypotenuse and so is on the triangle.

core.definition: In a triangle, the point where the three altitudes meet. It may lie inside, outside, or on the triangle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OR, with a lighter secondary stress on the sen syllable. American r is strong, and the final -er is a reduced r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term used in geometry classes and math writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say orthocenter in geometry and math class. The British spelling orthocentre is not used in American math writing. People talk about the orthocenter when discussing altitudes, which are the perpendicular lines drawn from each vertex to the opposite side.

distinctions.note: The centroid is the point where the medians meet, while the orthocenter is where the altitudes meet.
The circumcenter is the center of the circle through the three vertices, while the orthocenter is where the altitudes meet.

examples.everyday: My son asked why the three lines in his triangle drawing all cross at one point, and I told him it is the orthocenter.
examples.professional: For the mesh quality check, we flag any element where the orthocenter falls outside the triangle.
examples.analytical: The orthocenter, centroid, and circumcenter lie on the Euler line, a fact that reveals a hidden order in triangle geometry.

nuance.analogy: The orthocenter is like the point where three perpendicular posts from a triangle's corners all meet.
nuance.etymology: From Greek orthos meaning straight or right, plus center.
common_mistakes: Writing the British spelling orthocentre in American work.
Thinking the orthocenter is always inside the triangle, when it can be outside or on the triangle.

senses.definition: Of a set of vectors, both orthogonal and normalized.
